16 / The learning salon

Behind the scenes with AI

Real requests, real changes and lessons from this website. Even a digital salon needs an editor, testing and the occasional furniture rearrangement.

AI

How ideas became a website

This website is a collaboration between Miroslav Reiter, ChatGPT and Codex. Successive requests added humour, new pages, five languages, appearance modes and easier mobile controls.

Miroslav defines the purpose and requests specific changes. AI helps with design, writing, translation and code. Historical claims need sources, generated images need labels and the result needs human judgement.

The examples below are real excerpts from the author’s requests in this chat. We retain the original Slovak wording in every language edition and add a translation or explanation. This is not a complete conversation transcript.

Request: give it a spark

nech je to vtipné a zábavné ten web

Translation: make the website funny and entertaining.

Result: historical projects sit alongside TeaScript, a fictional modern CV, a salon advice column and AI beach scenes. Fiction is explicitly labelled.

Request: a more compact header

daj prepínače jazyka a vzhľadu vedľa seba do hlavičky, nech nezaberajú toľko miesta.

Translation: put the language and appearance switches next to each other in the header so they take up less space.

Result: language and appearance controls sit side by side. On mobile, the time machine, cards, advice and newspaper links moved into the menu. New learning pages are under Discover.

Request: the author’s real photograph

Na podstránku O stránke Ada pridaj aj moju fotografiu z webu VITA.

Translation: add my photograph from the VITA website to About Ada.

Result: About Ada contains the original VITA photograph, screen-reader text and a source link. The author’s portrait was not AI-generated.

Before and after the change

Real screenshots of earlier Slovak versions show the addition of the author’s photograph. Text inside the screenshots is Slovak; the captions are translated.

What we worked through

  1. The header took up too much space

    The author requested more compact controls. Shrinking the text was not enough: we put the switches on one row and moved extra mobile links into the menu.

  2. Emoji flags are not dependable everywhere

    The language picker needed flags that displayed on Windows too. We used separate SVG images alongside the language’s name and code.

  3. Visible text must match the accessible name

    Checks led us to adjust the controls’ screen-reader names so they included the visible language code. Good looks alone are not a sufficient usability check.

How we check the result

We check links, translation coverage, mobile layouts, keyboard controls and interactive behaviour. Source files and downloadable materials are kept in GitHub.

Automated checks do not replace a complete accessibility audit or expert review of every translation. The website does not claim full WCAG certification. Further updates address specific findings.
